catalog_quote: Within a large class of cases, the stress patterns of Passamaquoddy words can be predicted on the basis of two simple principles ...: (1) Initial Stress Rule (ISR) Stress the first syllable of a word. (2) Alternating Stress Rule (ASR) Stress the even-numbered syllables of a word, counting from right to left. ... the surface stress patterns of the language are much more complex than we would expect on the basis of these principles alone. ... Sometimes one or even two extra syllables must be skipped over in assigning alternating stress. ... I will refer to vowels which are "visible" to the stress rules ... as stressable vowels. Those vowels which are "invisible" to the stress rules -- whose presence is simply ignored in assigning stress -- I term unstressable vowels. ... sweep_summary: this search of works with stress in the title target has one item, LeSourd 1993 (Glottolog 162540), which is the catalog's own deciding source and is already held in full as the 1988 MIT thesis (text + full PDF). Re-read this search of works with stress in the title: the Abstract (p. 2), ch. 4 pp. 132-134 (Initial Stress Rule, right-to-left Alternating Stress Rule over stressable vowels only) and p. 143 (Main Stress Rule: rightmost stressed syllable is primary) confirm the catalog's weight-hedged coding verbatim. The 1993 Garland/Routledge print is paywalled (DOI 10.4324/9781315046785; T&F landing 403) but Crossref chapter records give its pagination ('Stress Assignment' segment pp. 87-95). No other stress/accent title for this language surfaced from Crossref;org/MUSE/JSTOR probes is incomplete. Extras: Olson 2018 (held) refines LeSourd (initial stress rarely realized in modern recordings; quantity-insensitive); Prince 1914 (downloaded from archive.org, pp. 95-96) has only an impressionistic intonation remark, silent on placement; Sherwood 1986 ch. 3 'Phonemics' (Maliseet) remains unread because the JSTOR open-access chapter is challenge-walled and MUSE serves no text (priority medium as the only unread first-hand phonology of the Maliseet half). Nothing read contradicts the catalog; no reclassification suggested. record:

new_statements.quote: Stress is assigned by a right-to-left alternating stress rule and a rule assigning stress to initial syllables; but the surface stress patterns of the language are more ccmplex than one would expect on the basis of these principles alone, since only stressable vowels participate in stress assignment. Matters are further complicated by the fact that particular underlying vowels which are treated as unstressable in some positions come to be treated as stressable when they occur in other contexts. [Abstract] ... Primary stress occurs on the rightmost stressed syllable of a word in pre-pausal position. This fact is stated as the Main Stress Rule (12). [p. 143]

new_statements.reading: Word stress is assigned by two default rules, initial stress and right-to-left alternating stress from the penult, but the count runs over stressable (full) vowels only; reduced/unstressable vowels are skipped, and primary stress goes to the rightmost stressed syllable. This is quantity-insensitive in the open/closed-syllable sense but sensitive to full-vs-reduced vowel visibility, i.e. exactly the catalog's 'weight-hedged' reading. Same work as the catalog's deciding source; the abstract gives a more compact statement of the ISR/ASR system than the pp. 132-134 quotation.

sources.citation: Olson, Erin. 2018 (ms.). Pitch accent drives stress placement in Passamaquoddy-Maliseet. MIT. [not a works with stress in the title; held secondary, re-read]
sources.quote: (1) Default stress pattern of Passamaquoddy-Maliseet (LeSourd, 1988, 1993): a. Stress is assigned to the first syllable of every word. b. Stress is assigned to every other syllable, starting on the penult and proceeding from right to left. c. Primary stress is generally held to be rightmost. ... when examining recordings from Language Keepers and Passamaquoddy-Maliseet Dictionary Project (2016) ... initial stress in these words is rarely present. ... These rules of stress assignment will create a strictly alternating stress pattern anchored on the penultimate syllable, counting from right to left. This stress pattern is quantity insensitive, so that both open and closed syllables behave identically with respect to stress.
sources.note: Restates LeSourd's default (initial + right-to-left alternating from the penult, rightmost primary), reports that the initial-stress rule is rarely realized in modern dictionary recordings, and calls the pattern quantity-insensitive apart from the invisibility of reduced vowels.

sources.note: Default pattern: initial-syllable stress plus right-to-left alternating stress counted over 'stressable' vowels only (unstressable vowels, mostly surface schwa and some i before y, are skipped); primary stress on the rightmost stressed syllable; morphologically specified final stress and Stress Shift in non-final forms complicate the surface. This is the catalog's own deciding source, re-read in the 1988 thesis text we hold layer; the 1993 Garland/Routledge print of the same work is paywalled (DOI 10.4324/9781315046785; T&F landing page 403 to download).

sources.quote: The intonation of the Passamaquoddy is highly tonic. Almost every accented syllable indicates a voice-lift. The voice is dropped on the syllable following the tone; half raised again on the third syllable and dropped again on the fourth: lakutwak'n; pronounced la kut wi k'n. This peculiarity appears to be distinctively Passamaquoddy, as the kindred Maliseets speak very monotonously and with no especially noticeable voice-lift on the accented syllable.
sources.note: Early impressionistic note on pitch on accented syllables and a Passamaquoddy/Maliseet difference; no rule for where word accent falls. Silent on placement.
